Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 62
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Stock Broker
  trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
  pcl5: 63

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Meaning: go over and over why the event happened to me, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
  Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
  Memory: Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear, Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory

Vignette:
Kofi Mensah is a 62-year-old Ghanaian-American stockbroker who presented for psychological evaluation following the sudden death of his son, Kwame, eight months prior. Divorced for nearly a decade and living alone in a high-rise apartment in Atlanta, Kofi had built his post-divorce life around two anchors: his work on the trading floor and his relationship with Kwame, who was 34 and had recently become a father himself. When Kwame collapsed without warning from a ruptured aortic aneurysm during a Sunday afternoon phone call — Kofi listening helplessly as the line went silent, then hearing his daughter-in-law's screaming in the background — the architecture of Kofi's world came apart in a way he has not been able to reconstruct.

In the weeks that followed, Kofi found himself unable to form a coherent account of what had happened. He knew, in the broadest outline, that his son had died. But the memory of that Sunday afternoon existed for him less as a continuous narrative than as a series of sharp, disconnected shards: the particular quality of Kwame's laugh just before the sound changed, the exact pitch of his daughter-in-law's voice, the sensation of the phone still warm in his hand. These fragments arrived without invitation — surfacing in the middle of a client call, or at two in the morning, vivid and sensory and then gone before he could examine them. When he tried deliberately to reconstruct the sequence of events — what had been said, how long he had stood there before calling back — he found the memory strangely inaccessible, as though he were reaching for something just beyond his grasp. He described this to his physician as feeling like he was only holding pieces of a photograph from which the most important part had been torn away.

There were moments, particularly in the early months, when the boundary between memory and present reality dissolved entirely. Standing at his trading terminal, watching a market index plunge, he would be overtaken by a sensation of being back inside that phone call — not remembering it, but inhabiting it, hearing the silence again, certain that something catastrophic was unfolding in real time. These episodes left him shaken and disoriented in ways he found deeply humiliating, and he had come to believe that his mind was no longer reliable in the way it once had been.

Kofi had quietly reorganized his life to minimize contact with anything that carried Kwame's imprint. He had not returned to the church they had attended together, had declined his daughter-in-law's invitations to see his granddaughter, and had removed the framed photographs from his apartment walls. The absence of those photographs had been noticed by a junior colleague who visited his office, and Kofi had offered a clipped explanation that invited no follow-up. His social world, already contracted by divorce, had narrowed further. He had simultaneously thrown himself into behaviors that alarmed the people around him: making aggressive, poorly researched trades that his supervisor had flagged twice in as many months, driving at speeds that he acknowledged were dangerous, as though the ordinary calculus of consequence no longer applied to him. What Kofi understood, in his more reflective moments, was that he had stopped being entirely certain why it mattered to be careful.

He spent considerable time trying to understand why this had happened to him specifically — rehearsing timelines, second-guessing conversations, wondering whether he had missed signs of illness in Kwame during their last visit. He also worked hard, and with limited success, to push these thoughts away when they arose, a project that left him exhausted and that he had come to associate with the persistent shame, anger, and fear that seemed to saturate his waking hours.

What finally brought Kofi to seek help was a call from his daughter-in-law asking whether he intended to be present for his granddaughter's first birthday. He had no answer. He arrived at the intake appointment composed and formally dressed, and what he said he most feared was that he would spend whatever years remained to him in a state of managed absence — present in body, unreachable in every way that mattered.
